title: Git Security Best Practices
description: Apply security best practices to protect your code, credentials, and collaborators.

data.text: Git security is not just about signing commits. It covers credential management, access control, repository hygiene, and incident response. Applying these best practices protects your code, your collaborators, and your organization.

items: **Never commit secrets**: Use .gitignore and tools like git-secrets or gitleaks to detect secrets
**Use environment variables**: Store API keys and tokens in environment variables, not in code
**Rotate credentials regularly**: Change passwords, tokens, and keys on a schedule
**Revoke immediately**: Revoke compromised credentials immediately and audit access logs

data.title: Scan for secrets in Git history
data.code:
# Install gitleaks (secrets scanner)
brew install gitleaks

# Scan the current repository
gitleaks detect --source . --report-path gitleaks-report.json

# Scan a specific commit range
gitleaks detect --source . --log-opts="--since=2024-01-01"

# Install git-secrets (AWS-focused scanner)
brew install git-secrets
git secrets --install

# Scan all commits
git secrets --scan-history

data.text: Use the principle of least privilege. Grant only the permissions necessary for a task. Use team-based access on GitHub and GitLab. Require PR reviews and branch protection for protected branches.

items: **Branch protection**: Require PR reviews and status checks before merge
**Required reviews**: Require at least one review for main/production branches
**Restrict force push**: Prevent force push on protected branches
**Token scoping**: Use fine-grained tokens with minimal permissions
**SSH key rotation**: Rotate keys every 90 days and on team member departure

data.text: Enable audit logs on GitHub and GitLab. Monitor for unusual activity: force pushes to protected branches, new SSH keys, and unexpected repository access. Set up alerts for security events.

data.title: GitHub security settings
data.code:
# Enable security features on GitHub:
# 1. Repository → Settings → Security → Code scanning → Set up
# 2. Enable Dependabot alerts
# 3. Enable Secret scanning
# 4. Enable Push protection

# Use GitHub CLI to list recent events
gh auth login
gh audit-log --limit 50

# Events to monitor:
# - git.push.force (force push)
# - git.ssh_key.add (new SSH key)
# - repo.settings_change (permission changes)
# - member.added (new collaborator)

data.text: Dependencies are a common attack vector. Use Dependabot or Renovate to keep dependencies up to date. Run npm audit or snyk test in CI. Pin dependency versions with lock files.

data.title: Dependency security in CI
data.code:
# Run security audit in CI
npm audit --audit-level=high

# Fail build on high/critical vulnerabilities
npm audit --audit-level=high || exit 1

# Use Snyk for deeper analysis
npx snyk test

# Enable Dependabot on GitHub
# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: npm
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    open-pull-requests-limit: 10

data.text: When a security incident occurs (leaked token, compromised account, malicious commit), respond quickly: revoke credentials, audit access, review recent commits, and rotate all exposed secrets.

items: **Audit**: Review access logs and recent commits for unauthorized activity
**Rotate**: Change all secrets that may have been exposed
**Notify**: Inform your team and affected users
**Remediate**: Remove malicious commits or revert changes if needed

data.title: Respond to a leaked token
data.code:
# Step 1: Revoke the token immediately
# GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Revoke

# Step 2: Audit recent commits
git log --since="24 hours ago" --oneline

# Step 3: Review GitHub audit log
gh audit-log --since="24 hours ago"

# Step 4: Rotate related secrets
# - Database passwords
# - API keys
# - SSH keys

# Step 5: Remove secret from Git history
# Use git filter-repo or BFG Repo-Cleaner
git filter-repo --path .env --invert-paths --force

# Step 6: Force push the cleaned history
git push --force origin main

# Step 7: Notify your team

data.title: Prevention is better than response
data.text: Implement preventive controls — secret scanning, Dependabot, branch protection — before an incident occurs. The cost of prevention is far lower than the cost of responding to a breach.

items.question: Can I use a pre-commit hook to block secrets?
items.answer: Yes. Use gitleaks or git-secrets as a pre-commit hook to scan for secrets before they are committed.

items.question: What if a secret was committed but not pushed?
items.answer: Amend the commit to remove the secret: git rm --cached <file> && git commit --amend. The secret is removed from the index. Rotate the secret anyway if it was exposed locally.

items.question: Does Git history rewriting affect open PRs?
items.answer: Yes. Force-pushing rewritten history updates the PR but may cause confusion. Coordinate with reviewers and use git push --force-with-lease for safety.

items.question: Can I recover from a compromised GitHub account?
items.answer: Yes. Enable 2FA, review and revoke all sessions and tokens, check audit logs for unauthorized access, and notify GitHub support if needed.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use gitleaks or git-secrets to scan for secrets in Git history
Enable Dependabot and Secret scanning on GitHub
Use branch protection and required PR reviews
Revoke and rotate credentials immediately after a leak
Implement preventive controls before an incident occurs
